How this feed is made

Underneath it is a database of daily price history for several thousand companies listed on the NASDAQ and NYSE, going back years. Those companies are organised two ways at once: by the public sector and industry classifications everyone uses, and by hand — into roughly 250 groups drawn from news reports, podcasts and industry deep dives, which cut across the official taxonomy in ways it never would. Layered on top are forward analyst projections and the transcripts of recent earnings calls. Holding all of it in one place is the point: it means every brief is grounded in primary, verifiable data — prices as the exchange reported them, fundamentals drawn from company filings, and what management actually said on the call — rather than in whatever a search happens to surface. Where the database cannot answer a question, the agents do search the web — with a blocklist that strips out sites publishing volume rather than insight, and a standing instruction to prefer primary sources and filings, or to drop a fact rather than source it badly.

The newsroom. Three automated agents run in sequence, imitating how a real desk works:

  1. The Hypothesizer reads a daily snapshot of what moved and what changed direction, and proposes one question worth chasing.
  2. The Investigator goes and checks — querying the price database, reading company fundamentals and research notes, and searching the web — then reports back with evidence.
  3. The Editor scores that evidence. Weak stories are spiked; strong ones are written up as the article you are reading.

The Editor is instructed to observe, never to advise — so you will not find buy or sell calls here.

Accenture and Cognizant Added Staff All Year, and Revenue Per Employee Rose Just 2%

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Generative AI is supposed to be deflating the billable hour at the big systems integrators. The one disclosure that would show it, revenue per head, has barely moved at Accenture or Cognizant, and both are still hiring.

Accenture closed fiscal 2026 with record new bookings of $84.54bn, a wider operating margin and about 35,000 more employees. Cognizant's reported third-quarter growth of 4.6% was almost all acquisitions and resold third-party product, leaving organic services growth under 1%.

Accenture holds the better operating record: margin expansion on a 1.2 book-to-bill. Cognizant cut its constant-currency growth guidance for the year to 4.0-4.4% and signed 7% fewer bookings in the quarter than a year earlier. Output per head, derived from each company's own filings, improved roughly 2% at both.

Accenture, the Dublin-headquartered firm selling strategy, consulting, cloud, data and multi-year managed operations to large enterprises, closed its fiscal year on 31 August with record new bookings, a wider operating margin and roughly 35,000 more people on the payroll than a year earlier. That last fact is the problem with the story the sector has been sold.

The case against the big integrators, stated plainly in the note that reinstated coverage of Cognizant at Neutral in mid-November, is that artificial intelligence is a structural rather than cyclical headwind, because it erodes billable hours and pushes delivery risk onto the vendor. The case for them is that the same tools let a firm bill the same work with fewer people. Both arguments resolve to one measurable quantity: revenue per employee. Derived from each company's reported revenue and its own disclosed headcount, it moved about 2% at each over the past year.

Accenture's margin gain was made below the delivery line

Revenue of $74.18bn was up 6.5% in fiscal 2026, operating income up 11.5%, and the operating margin reached 15.4% against 14.7%. That is real operating leverage, and it did not come from the price of the work: gross margin was flat at 32.1%. Headcount reached approximately 814,000 at 31 August against approximately 779,000 a year earlier, a 4.5% rise set against revenue growth of 6.5%, leaving output per head at roughly $91,100 from $89,400. Voluntary attrition rose to 14% from 13%, so nobody is leaving faster either. The firm booked $923m of restructuring charges in the year under a programme that reskills some people and exits others where reskilling is not viable.

The order book is the strongest part of the record: new bookings of $84.54bn for the year, a record, up 5% in dollars and 3% in local currency, with a trailing four-quarter managed-services book-to-bill of 1.2 and 141 client bookings above $100m in the fourth quarter. Managed services supplied $12.77bn of that quarter's $22.17bn, so most of what was signed is contracted run-work priced before the hours are worked.

What is no longer in the record is the AI line. Accenture retired its separate advanced-AI bookings disclosure after the first quarter of fiscal 2026, the final print being $2.2bn of bookings and about $1.1bn of revenue, on the grounds that advanced AI is now embedded in nearly everything it does. A client count replaced it: more than 400 clients initiated advanced-AI work during the year. "AI is the breakthrough innovation. Only reinvention can unlock the value," chief executive Julie Sweet said at the 14 October investor day, where the firm also said its AI and data workforce had grown from 40,000 to nearly 110,000 professionals over four years, additive to the 814,000 rather than a substitution for it.

Cognizant's 4.6% was mostly bought and resold

Cognizant, the Teaneck firm selling consulting, technology and outsourcing to financial services, healthcare, products and communications clients, grew third-quarter revenue 4.6% to $5.664bn. Acquisitions contributed roughly 2.1 percentage points of that and resale of third-party products roughly 1.9, leaving organic services growth under 1%. Headcount of 359,900 was up 2.9% year on year, putting revenue per employee near $60,800 from $59,600.

The adjusted operating margin of 16.3% was the highest in four years and a seventh consecutive quarter of year-on-year expansion. The reported margin went the other way, 15.4% against 16.0%. Guidance for constant-currency growth was cut to 4.0-4.4% from 4.0-5.5% on discretionary pressure in healthcare and consumer-facing sectors, and bookings signed in the quarter fell 7% even as the trailing-twelve-month total rose 4% to $28.7bn on a 1.3x book-to-bill. "Even at midpoint of 4.2%, we would be both on total growth basis as well as on the organic basis would be delivering a top-tier performance vis-à-vis rest of the players," chief financial officer Jatin Dalal told investors on 29 October. Deutsche Bank cut the stock to Hold on 13 November, target $66 from $75, saying its growth thesis had not played out.

One mechanism here points the right way. Fixed-price and transaction-based work reached 58% of revenue, up 1.4 points year on year and 5 points since the third quarter of 2022, the contract form under which a productivity gain stays with the vendor. "The pivot is switching from productivity to growth imperatives using AI. And the rebaselining of productivity has already happened to a large extent," chief executive Ravi Kumar said on the same call. At 10.6x forward earnings, the shares carry about a third less than the 15.3x on which the equivalent forward estimate was priced two years ago.

What the per-head numbers settle

Neither income statement carries the deflation yet, in either direction.

Six months of share gains, Accenture up 31.8% and Cognizant up 18.7%, came with no acceleration underneath them. Accenture's quarterly revenue growth ran between 5.6% and 8.3% through the year and its fiscal 2027 guidance is 3% to 6% in local currency; Cognizant decelerated from 5.8% to 4.6% across three quarters. Both then handed much of the gain back in a market-wide correction driven by a December Federal Reserve rate hike moving to roughly 95% probability, with no company disclosure behind it.

Accenture is being paid more per client without getting more out of each employee, and part of the next leg is bought: the investor-day framework has acquisitions contributing 2% to 2.5% of fiscal 2027 revenue against roughly 1.5% in fiscal 2026. Its 17.1x trailing earnings against 15.9x forward prices about 7% earnings growth, well under the 27.8x forward the shares carried two years ago. Cheap because slow, in other words, and the slowness is in the guidance.

The threat neither filing captures arrived from above. Anthropic, whose Claude models roughly 30,000 Accenture professionals are trained to deploy, launched its own consulting and professional-services division on 3 November, and OpenAI has made a similar move. The model vendors now bid for the implementation work, and the integrators' answer, for the moment, is to hire.

The setup

Would confirmCognizant's fourth-quarter growth landing inside 3.2-4.7% with acquisitions and product resale again supplying most of it.
Would invalidateAccenture revenue per employee above roughly $93,000 at fiscal 2027 year-end with headcount at or below 814,000.
Watch nextCognizant's fourth-quarter report against its 3.2-4.7% constant-currency guide, which includes roughly 2 points from acquisitions.

Credo's Threat Is MaxLinear's Cable Silicon; Astera Labs' Is One Customer at 53%

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Two makers of the silicon that moves bits between accelerators inside an artificial-intelligence rack have been marked down together since late October on one shared worry, that copper links are about to be designed out of the rack. The order books say the two risks are nothing alike.

Credo's decline dates to 22 October, when MaxLinear's chief executive told analysts Credo holds an estimated 93% to 99% of the active electrical cable market and that MaxLinear wants 20% to 30% of the 1.6-terabit generation, with first revenue in 2027. Astera Labs had no such event: revenue grew 154% year on year in the September quarter and operating margin reached 30.6%, and the shares still fell about a quarter in 30 days.

The pricing is now the reverse of the growth. Credo, decelerating, trades at 17.0x forward earnings; Astera, accelerating, at 43.5x — while its largest customer went from 23% to 53% of quarterly revenue in a year.

Two companies sell the wiring that carries bits between accelerators inside an artificial-intelligence rack, and since late October the market has marked them down together on a single stated worry: that copper links are about to be designed out in favor of optics. Only one of them had something happen to its business. Credo Technology, which builds retimed copper cables, the signal-processing chips inside them and the serializer-deserializer circuits it also licenses, lost a fifth of its market value across two sessions in October after a competitor told investors it intends to take a share of the market Credo almost entirely owns.

The read-across to Astera Labs, which sells retimers, smart cable modules and the Scorpio fabric switches that connect accelerators over PCI Express and newer scale-up fabrics, assumed one architectural clock governs both. Astera's own September quarter argues against it. Revenue grew 154% year on year to $584.9m, and operating margin reached 30.6% against 20.1% two quarters earlier. The shares fell 23% in the two sessions after that print.

The 93% MaxLinear wants a piece of

On MaxLinear's 22 October call, chief executive Kishore Seendripu put Credo's share of the active electrical cable market at an estimated 93% to 99% and said his company would sell silicon to cable manufacturers rather than build finished cables, targeting 20% to 30% of the 1.6-terabit segment, with first revenue in 2027 and volume in 2028. Credo fell 10.9% that day and 9.5% the next, on roughly double its normal volume. MaxLinear is not posturing from a standing start: its quarterly revenue reached $218.1m, up 72% year on year, with infrastructure up 210% on optical data-center products.

Credo's stated defense is integration. Asked at Goldman Sachs's Communacopia conference on 10 September whether new entrants were gaining traction, chief executive Bill Brennan said the company had "decided to own the entire system solution" and that "we're the single throat to choke when it comes to delivering the SKUs that our customer wants", calling that his biggest competitive moat.

The numbers around it are mixed. Sequential revenue growth has settled near 10%, from 51.9% in the January quarter. Gross margin on a reported basis fell to 64.5% in the August quarter from 68.2%, and operating income declined sequentially to $120.7m on higher revenue. But concentration loosened rather than tightened: the top four customers were 84% of revenue, with a new 10% customer added, against roughly 88% for the top three a year and a half earlier. The December-quarter guide of $525m to $535m beat consensus, the fiscal-2027 guide of more than 85% growth is intact, and management reiterated more than $600m of that year's revenue coming from optics, including silicon-photonics chips and optical signal processors.

Astera's risk sits in the customer file

Astera is the only one of the two that prices the rack in dollars. "Today, our content per XPU across fabric switches and copper signal conditioning can exceed $1,000 per XPU," chief executive Jitendra Mohan said on the 3 November call, adding that Scorpio "became our largest product family in Q3" at more than $1bn in annualized revenue. President and chief operating officer Sanjay Gajendra said "fully loaded Orion rack scale designs contain greater than $100,000 in Astera Labs content."

What the selloff can fairly point at is in the 10-Q, not the growth rate. Customer A was 53% of quarterly revenue against 23% a year earlier, and 58% of receivables. Inventory rose to $200.9m from $59.0m at the end of 2025. And Amazon's Trainium4 incorporates both NVLink Fusion and UALink, a move away from the PCI Express network that carried Scorpio in Trainium3.

The multiples run backwards to the growth

Credo trades at 17.0x forward earnings and 12.0x forward gross profit, against 50.5x trailing gross profit in May 2026; its market value has fallen from $36.6bn to $20.1bn while trailing gross profit more than doubled. Astera, after falling nearly as far, is still 43.5x forward earnings and 22.0x forward gross profit, roughly 1.8x Credo on both, from 52.3x trailing gross profit in May on a near-identical market value.

So the decelerating business carries the cheaper multiple and the accelerating one the dearer, which is the opposite of what a shared architecture scare would produce.

Most of the November leg was not about cables at all. Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia chief executive on 12 November, the 20 November session in which the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.28% with the volatility index at 35.89, and his reinstatement on 23 November moved both names in lockstep with the index; Marvell, down 36.7% over the same 30 days on its all-stock Lumentum deal, fell further than either. Within that, Credo's two-day October fall is the only company-specific repricing on the shelf, and it discounts a 2028 volume event. Astera's analyst cuts were to targets, not estimates. Meanwhile Nvidia's Rubin Ultra rack, due in the second half of 2027, connects its 144 accelerators over an all-copper scale-up network, and co-packaged optics arrives for scale-up in 2027 and 2028, possibly alongside copper first.

Credo reports its fiscal second quarter after the close on 1 December, the first disclosure since a rival named a number for its market. The useful line will not be the revenue beat but the customer table: the company that just added a fifth ten-percent buyer is the one being priced as though it is about to lose one.

Where it standsBoth are down roughly a quarter in 30 days; Credo's decline dates to MaxLinear's 22 October share claim, Astera's to after a record quarter.

The software duopoly that designs the world's semiconductors was marked down this month on a single question: whether hyperscale computing budgets keep paying for chip design. What the two companies' filings show is that the more contracted of the pair is the smaller one. Cadence Design Systems, which sells simulation, synthesis and sign-off tools plus Palladium emulation hardware and design IP, booked 79% of its September-quarter revenue as recurring and 21% upfront, against 82% and 18% a year earlier.

That matters because the ranking is usually read the other way. Synopsys, the larger business, has long been described as the ratable one: multi-year time-based licenses for its electronic-design-automation tools, with hardware and silicon IP as the lumpy edge. Its third-quarter filing says time-based products were 40% of the July quarter's $2.477bn, down from 53% of revenue a year earlier, with upfront products at 27%. The de-rating is landing on already-signed backlog at one name and on delivery-timed revenue at the other.

Ansys moved the Synopsys dollar off the ratable line

The mechanism is in the acquired company's own accounting. Ansys recognizes its multi-year subscription lease licenses up front at lease commencement, a practice Ansys said makes revenue "more volatile" and the reason it reported annual contract value separately. Synopsys closed the deal in 2025; Ansys contributed $622.2m of the third quarter's revenue increase, and roughly $2.98bn of guided fiscal-2026 revenue.

The rest of the dollar moved with it. Of Synopsys's $10.9bn backlog, excluding $1.9bn of non-cancellable commitments, about 49% is expected in revenue over the next twelve months — nine percentage points less forward conversion than Cadence. Gross margin was 72.6% in the quarter against 78.1% a year earlier. Organic growth in the design-software business slowed to 8.5%, a deceleration Morgan Stanley had flagged in a downgrade, and the $10.0bn of senior notes that financed the purchase cost $429.3m of interest over nine months. Design IP did return to growth, up about 11%.

None of this is order weakness. The sequential dip in backlog was attributed to the sale of the processor IP business, which GlobalFoundries completed on 2 June 2026.

Cadence's upfront line is building supply into orders

Cadence's lumpy segment is doing the opposite of clearing. Its chief financial officer commentary says inventories were raised specifically to work through a significant emulation order backlog, with no current capacity or supply constraints. "Q3 revenue grew 22% year-over-year, with strong double-digit growth across all product categories, driven by growing momentum from AI-driven designs," John Wall, chief financial officer, said on 26 October. Recurring revenue grew 18%, double the prior year's 11%, and full-year guidance went to 21% revenue growth with the earnings target up $0.30 to $8.40.

China, the exposure usually invoked to explain either discount, is the larger line at Cadence — 16% of the quarter, down from 18% — against 10% at Synopsys.

Both are also digesting a simulation deal. Cadence completed its purchase of Hexagon's Design & Engineering business on 23 February 2026 for about €2.7bn, adding roughly $160m of 2026 revenue at minimal operating profit and about 28 cents of dilution before turning accretive in 2027.

The cheaper earnings sit with the lumpier revenue

Cadence trades at 31.2x consensus fiscal-2027 earnings of $9.85, against roughly 50x forward in late July. Synopsys is at 22.7x the 2027 consensus of $18.84.

Shares in both are well below their highs of the past year — Synopsys by 20%, Cadence by 26% — so the markdown predates November. The month's move is concentrated in two sessions: both fell about 8% on 20 November, when the Nasdaq Composite wiped out its 2026 gain and Nvidia dropped 14% despite record revenue, then rebounded 8% to 9% on 23 November. No disclosure specific to either company sits on those dates.

The quantified bear case is a customer-budget case rather than a backlog case: Bank of America estimates that holding cloud spending near current levels implies roughly a 20% cut to projected capital expenditure and 35% to 40% downside to artificial-intelligence semiconductor earnings. That would reach tool renewals eventually. It has not reached them yet: Cadence's $4.2bn of revenue expected from contracted obligations over the next twelve months is already signed, core tools grew 20%, IP 24% and system design 30%, and the board authorized a further $2.5bn of repurchases after buying $400m of stock in the quarter.

So the results account for Synopsys's discount and not for Cadence's. Synopsys pays for its lower multiple with mix, margin and leverage; its headline 42% revenue growth is acquisition arithmetic sitting on 8.5% organic expansion. Cadence pays a premium for a dollar that arrives on contract, and that dollar grew faster this quarter than last. The demand both managements point to is physical. "TSMC showed their process road map and said in the next 5 years, the chip size will go up by 48x. 48x," chief executive Anirudh Devgan told investors on 26 October, explaining why verification hardware keeps selling.

Synopsys has not spoken to the market since 26 August, when chief executive Sassine Ghazi said "AI is driving unprecedented complexity and increasing demand for the silicon IP and engineering solutions necessary to deliver next-generation AI compute." Its fourth-quarter and fiscal-year results land after the close on 8 December — the first test of whether the organic tool growth management promised would reach double digits in the quarter actually did.

The setup

Where it standsCadence books 79% of revenue as recurring with record $8.2bn backlog; Synopsys's ratable share fell to 40% as the Ansys book recognizes upfront.
Would confirmCadence recurring share near 79% and backlog at or above $8.2bn at the next report, with twelve-month conversion holding near 58%.
Would invalidateCadence backlog below $8bn or recurring share under 75%, or Synopsys organic design-software growth below 8.5% in the December print.
Watch nextSynopsys fourth-quarter and fiscal 2026 results after the close on 8 December 2026, its first update since 26 August.
ValuationCadence at 36.6x fiscal-2026 and 31.2x fiscal-2027 consensus earnings, against roughly 50x forward in late July; Synopsys at 28.2x and 22.7x.

Gentex Keeps Selling More Electronics Per Car While the Market Prices It With Robotaxis

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

A mirror maker shipped far fewer mirrors last quarter and barely lost any car revenue, because the content it fits on each vehicle it still supplies went up. That is the whole defense, and it is now colliding with a component bill repricing faster than Gentex can pass it through.

Gentex shipped 9.61m auto-dimming mirrors in the September quarter, down 14.5% from a year earlier, while automotive revenue fell only 3.7% to $552.5m. Gross margin still slipped 100 basis points to 33.4%, and management flagged $10-15m of additional fourth-quarter costs it does not expect to recover until the first half of 2027.

The stock is priced on the same shelf as Mobileye and Hesai, where the autonomy story has been marked down hard. Gentex is not in that trade: its revenue follows build rates and content wins, and it trades at 9.8x forward earnings against roughly 16.6x two years ago while consensus earnings rose.

Forward fiscal years only. Blank means no analyst coverage for that year.

Gentex, which builds the electrochromic auto-dimming rearview mirrors, driver-monitoring cameras and full display mirrors that carmakers fit from Zeeland, Michigan, shipped 9.612m mirror units in the September quarter. That is 14.5% fewer than a year earlier, and its automotive revenue fell 3.7%, to $552.5m. Dividing one into the other gives roughly $57.5 of automotive revenue per mirror shipped, against about $51.0 a year ago — a derived figure, and the entire explanation for why a seventh of the unit base went missing without the revenue following.

That gap is the business. Gentex is classified among autonomous-driving and vehicle-electronics suppliers, and over the twelve months to 23 November its shares fell 12.8% while mainstream parts makers in the same table rose — Magna 27.3%, BorgWarner 16.3%. The markdown has been read as autonomy being de-rated. Gentex's revenue is not set by autonomy at all: it is set by how many cars get built and how much equipment the company fits inside each one.

The content wins are real; the component bill is repricing faster

North American automotive revenue rose about 3% against a 5% decline in regional light-vehicle production, and European revenue rose 13% excluding a lost Volkswagen program. Driver and in-cabin monitoring and full display mirror take rates did that work. "This acceleration in growth is being driven by new technology, higher content per vehicle, and a more diversified customer base," chief executive Steven Downing told investors on 23 October, explaining a reaffirmed 2027 revenue range of $2.8-2.9bn — 6-9% growth against primary markets the company expects to shrink about 1%.

The cost side moved the other way. Gross margin fell 100 basis points to 33.4% on precious-metal inflation and weaker operating leverage, and 2026 revenue guidance came down to about $2.65bn after a roughly $35m hit from a Hyundai/Kia union strike that landed mid-launch. Then there is memory, already the story of this quarter across electronics hardware.

"Anywhere from 8x to 10x price increases on a per unit basis. So I mean, literally, a component that cost $4 or $5 this earlier this year is now $40," Downing said on the same call, describing DDR memory and raw printed-circuit-board supply. Guidance carries $10-15m of incremental fourth-quarter cost with recovery not expected until the first half of 2027.

The two names beside it are not having the same quarter

Mobileye, which sells EyeQ vision chips and higher-content assisted-driving stacks, shipped 9.5m EyeQs, up 3.3%, at a $49.10 average system price against $51.70 a year earlier; gross profit still rose 7.4% on revenue down 2.4%, and full-year guidance went up. The shares fell 57% over twelve months, to 0.48x book. Hesai, the Shanghai lidar maker, shipped 729,673 units, up 65.3%, for 34.3% more revenue — about 19% less revenue per unit — with gross margin at 41.0% against 42.1% and fourth-quarter guidance implying growth of roughly 10-15%.

So one shelf holds three different problems. Mobileye's economics improved while its price halved. Hesai is buying platform share with price and watching operating income fall as units compound. Gentex is the only one whose units and margin both genuinely deteriorated, and the only one whose fix is already contracted: content per car, won years ago, landing now.

Its de-rating is a multiple. Forward earnings are capitalized at 9.8x against roughly 16.6x two years ago, while consensus earnings over that span rose; the stock carries a 7.0x enterprise value to EBITDA and an 11.2% trailing free-cash-flow yield. Gentex repurchased 5.7m shares in the quarter at an average $23.44, about a fifth above the 23 November price of $19.54.

The mirror count will likely keep falling as build rates drift lower, which means content per car has to keep outrunning it. The awkward part is that the cheapest items on the bill of materials are the ones repricing — and Downing said the fourth-generation full display mirror is being designed to need no DDR memory at all.

The setup

Where it standsMirror units down 14.5% year over year, automotive revenue down 3.7%, 2026 revenue guidance cut to about $2.65bn, 2027 range reaffirmed.
Would confirmAutomotive revenue per mirror unit holding near $57.5 and gross margin recovering above 33.4% as cost pass-throughs land.
Would invalidateRevenue per mirror unit falling back toward $51, or the $2.8-2.9bn 2027 revenue range being cut.
Watch nextFourth-quarter results carrying the $10-15m of incremental component costs management said would not be recovered until the first half of 2027.

Two outsourced chip assemblers were marked down together this month as one bet on advanced packaging being the bottleneck in artificial-intelligence hardware. The week of 17 November split them on the thing that pays: a signed capacity commitment.

ASE Technology's subsidiary Siliconware Precision Industries agreed with Nvidia to triple Nvidia-dedicated turnkey packaging lines in Taiwan by mid-2029. Siliconware Precision Industries, the packaging subsidiary of ASE Technology Holding, signed a multibillion-dollar, multi-year agreement with Nvidia on 17-18 November covering turnkey advanced packaging lines in Taiwan — bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and test — intended to triple Nvidia-dedicated capacity by mid-2029. Amkor Technology, the Tempe assembler that counted Apple as 29.8% of 2025 revenue and Qualcomm as 11.1%, has been brought in as a third supplier of 2.5-dimensional packaging and remains in early-stage collaboration, with engineering runs and pilot production but no meaningful volume expected in 2027, Digitimes reported on 23 November.

That reorders a hierarchy the market had taken for granted. Earlier this year the assumption was that TSMC's chip-on-wafer-on-substrate capacity was the binding constraint on accelerator output and that the independent assemblers were its overflow valve, with Amkor first in line as the non-Taiwanese second source. Both names have since been sold as one trade. The disclosures separate them on the only measure that matters: what a finished package pays.

One leading-edge package pays ASE three times what the electronics business does

ASE's assembly, test and materials segment turned over TWD 151.5bn in the September quarter, up 51% year over year, on a 30.6% gross margin and a 20% operating margin. That segment is 62% of consolidated revenue and 91% of group operating profit. The electronics manufacturing arm, whose volumes still grew 35%, ran an 8.3% gross margin after component pass-through costs, down from 8.9% in the June quarter. Consolidated revenue overstates the franchise; the segment table corrects it completely.

"The so-called structural margin ceiling has now become the base for us," chief financial officer Joseph Tung told investors on 29 October. Leading-edge advanced packaging revenue was guided above $4bn for 2026, up from $3.7bn mid-call, and Tung said ASE expects "to double our LEAP revenue" in 2027. Full-process CoWoS goes from $300m this year to above $1bn next; co-packaged optics is guided above $0.5bn in 2027. Utilization is at or near 100%, with physical space rather than demand named as the constraint, and capital spending was raised to roughly $11.5bn against net debt-to-equity of 66%.

Amkor's mix turned over while its revenue stood still

Amkor's September quarter was a profit record on a flat top line: revenue up 0.18% year over year after 25.6% growth in the June quarter, with gross profit up 27.8% and operating income up 41.4% as gross margin reached 18.26% from 14.32%. Communications fell to 37% of revenue from 51%, Computing rose 25% sequentially to a record on a high-density fan-out processor program, and automotive and industrial grew 37%. Advanced products were $1.632bn of $1.991bn in net sales, about 82%. The handset weakness is an artifact of memory: DRAM wafers diverted to high-bandwidth stacks starved the system-in-package line of components.

Amkor is spending into the gap. It committed $1.3bn to Korea on 21 October, taking multi-year commitments with Nvidia to roughly $3bn, and has taken about $3bn of advance payments from a dozen customers against future capacity, enough to fund capex without new debt through 2027. Arizona Phase 1 completes late 2027. "Customers are not only planning further ahead, but are also making long-term commitments," chief executive Kevin Engel said on 26 October.

What reaches either company is the cheaper end. TrendForce reported in August that CoWoS-R and CoWoS-S are the processes being released first, and HBM stacking stays inside the memory makers, from through-silicon-via fill to final test.

Two sessions, both market-wide, did the damage

Over the month to 23 November Amkor fell 11.4% and ASE 17.6%. Compound 5 November and 20 November alone and the declines are 24.3% and 31.1% — more than the full-month moves. Those were the two worst sessions in the market this month, the first on the post-midterm turn against artificial-intelligence capital spending plus Qualcomm's 26% drop in handset chip revenue, the second on a reported SEC probe of Nvidia. Neither day carried a disclosure from either assembler. On 23 November, with Jensen Huang reinstated, Amkor rose 15.1% and ASE 21.4% against a market mean of 3.3%.

So the month's selling says nothing about packaging economics; the week's contracts say a great deal. Amkor trades at 13.9x trailing earnings and 12.6x FY2027 consensus EPS of $2.76, against 44.4x in May on a market value that has gone from $19.1bn to $8.6bn, with nothing worse than flat revenue behind it. ASE sits at 30.2x trailing against 52.6x in May, but its market value has fallen only about 6% since then while trailing earnings nearly doubled: the de-rating is earnings arriving at a price that stood still.

Amkor's Arizona plant finishes its first phase in late 2027 — the same year the wafers it has not yet qualified to run start shipping from Taiwan.

The setup

Where it standsASE's packaging unit holds a signed Nvidia capacity agreement and 30.6% segment margins; Amkor posts record profit on flat revenue and pilot-stage 2.5D work.
Would confirmASE assembly-and-test gross margin holding at or above 30% with fourth-quarter segment revenue up 11-13% sequentially as guided.
Would invalidateAmkor qualifying 2.5D volume production in 2027, or ASE segment margin falling back below the high-20s on pricing.

Congress's Stopgap Keeps Paying AeroVironment and Kratos While Red Cat Waits for Funding

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

The same markdown landed on three American drone makers this month, and only one of them had an order book that actually deteriorated. AeroVironment reported record funded backlog of $1.5bn, up 37% from a year earlier, on a 1.4 book-to-bill and reaffirmed fiscal 2027 revenue guidance of $2.125–2.225bn. Kratos booked $1.04bn in its third quarter for a 2.2:1 book-to-bill and a record $2.6bn backlog, $2.07bn of it funded.

Red Cat is the exception: it withdrew its 2026 revenue target on 16 November after missing the Army's Gauntlet II cut, with quarterly revenue of $11.77m against roughly $40.7m expected and gross margin of 0.6%.

The stopgap running the Pentagon pays programs already funded and bars new starts. That protects the two larger names and strands the one whose revenue sits in an unfunded pipeline.

The rule governing Pentagon money until 11 December pays for last year's programs and forbids starting new ones, and that clause of appropriations law separates three listed drone makers more cleanly than their business descriptions do. AeroVironment, which builds Switchblade loitering munitions and, since its BlueHalo purchase, space and directed-energy systems, is paid largely on reorders of things the Army already buys. So is Kratos, the target-drone, hypersonics and satellite-software contractor. Red Cat, which supplies reconnaissance and first-person-view drones to government buyers, needs orders that have not been funded yet.

All three were marked down as one trade. Over the thirty days to 23 November AeroVironment fell 26.4%, Kratos 26.3% and Red Cat 57.3%, while the primes sat still: General Dynamics was off 0.4%, L3Harris up 0.3%, Lockheed Martin down 5.4%. The reading embedded in that gap is that unmanned systems are a budget bet and the budget is stuck. Two of the three order books say the opposite.

The stopgap bars starts, not deliveries

The continuing resolution holds defense at the extended fiscal 2026 baseline of $838.5bn against a $1.5 trillion request, and bars any program not already funded and active in the prior year. Breaking Defense counted more than 150 fiscal 2027 initiatives blocked from starting, including $17.5bn of Golden Dome missile-defense work. The Senate Appropriations Committee finished releasing draft text for all twelve fiscal 2027 bills on 16 November, but floor action on the defense authorization is unlikely before December and the odds of a year-long Pentagon stopgap have risen. A rule like that is close to neutral for a contractor shipping against funded orders and punitive for one waiting on an award.

AeroVironment's consumables keep being reordered

AeroVironment's first fiscal 2027 quarter brought record funded backlog of $1.5bn, up 37% year on year, with $1.4bn unfunded and a 1.4 book-to-bill; Precision Strike revenue, the loitering-munition and counter-drone line, was $197m, up 8%. The Army placed a $51m delivery order for additional Switchblade 600 Block 2 systems on 26 August, and in November the company took a $405m international order for LOCUST X3 high-energy laser counter-drone systems, a BlueHalo line whose economics rest on power and thermal limits rather than magazine depth. Guidance was reaffirmed at $2.125–2.225bn of revenue and $305–325m of adjusted EBITDA on 9 September. "AV's fiscal year 2027 is off to a strong start, with record first-quarter revenue and funded backlog and landmark strategic wins," chairman and chief executive Wahid Nawabi said that day.

The damage in the accounts is older and identifiable. The Satellite Communication Augmentation Resource contract acquired with BlueHalo, grown to roughly $1.7bn, was terminated on 10 March 2026, producing a $240.7m goodwill write-down and a $243.8m quarterly net loss. That is why the trailing earnings multiple is negative and useless. On forward estimates the shares trade at 2.09x sales, against roughly 6x a year ago on the same revenue base, 27.7x forward earnings and 1.03x book.

Kratos guided below its own internal plan

Kratos grew third-quarter revenue 35.7% to $471.8m and booked $1.037bn, leaving $2.067bn of funded and $582.9m of unfunded backlog. Its initial 2027 guide of $2.10–2.20bn assumes an unchanged $1.15 trillion authorization topline and the stopgap resolved by 31 March. "Kratos' internal 2027 revenue and EBITDA financial forecast currently rolls up considerably higher than what we are initially guiding to today, with a substantial part of the 2027 forecast supported by programs of record," chief executive Eric DeMarco told investors on 5 November. Cost-plus work rose to 32% of revenue from 22–23%, which caps margin at roughly a point of expansion next year, and management does not expect positive cash flow until 2029. The competitive hole is real: the Air Force gave collaborative combat aircraft Increment 1 production to Anduril and General Atomics in June, and Kratos is competing in Increment 2. At 2.99x forward sales, against about 12x enterprise value to revenue in May, and 33.7x forward earnings, the de-rating has answered the valuation objection without touching the backlog.

Red Cat's revenue sat in the unfunded column

Red Cat withdrew its 2026 revenue target on 16 November, saying anticipated funding and awards had progressed more slowly than expected and that the Army's Gauntlet II outcome removed an expected near-term contributor. Its first-person-view entry scored top of the field on production capability but weak in low-light and subterranean flight; at Fort Carson, operators flew 1,858 sorties across 23 platforms from 19 companies, with Perennial Autonomy and Neros leading. Quarterly revenue was $11.77m against roughly $40.7m expected, gross margin 0.6% against 6.6%, on scrap, warranty and factory overhead no shipments absorbed. Nine-month operating cash burn was $156.8m, inventory went to $117.2m from $23.5m, and diluted shares reached 136.9m from 99.6m. Chief executive Jeffrey Thompson put the pipeline for the maritime unit at "approximately $2.3 billion" on the 16 November call, of which he described roughly $250m funded in the United States, and described the first customer for it: "We splashed our first boat last December and 11 months later, we have our first customer." With $242.7m of cash against a $289m market value, the floor argument is the balance sheet.

What the quarters explain and what they do not

For AeroVironment and Kratos the fall is compression of a multiple against order books that grew, and the sharpest leg was not theirs: the Nasdaq Composite fell about 10% in the week to 20 November, its worst week since March 2020, on doubts about artificial-intelligence capital spending, and small-cap defense technology went with it. Nothing the two companies disclosed in that window was financial. For Red Cat the markdown is earned, and the cause of the split is structural: replenishment of a munition already in the budget and a funded production backlog convert under a stopgap, while a pipeline of letters of request and a Taiwanese tender for 1,320 unmanned surface vessels, award expected in March 2027, does not.

AeroVironment reports its second fiscal-quarter results in early December, days from the stopgap's expiry. Funded backlog gets paid through a lapse; the companies whose revenue is still an opportunity do not.

The setup

Where it standsAeroVironment and Kratos hold record funded backlogs and reaffirmed guidance; Red Cat has withdrawn its 2026 revenue target after the Gauntlet II miss.
Would confirmAeroVironment's early-December quarter showing funded backlog and book-to-bill above 1.0 with guidance intact; Red Cat revenue still near $12m a quarter.
Would invalidateAeroVironment trimming fiscal 2027 revenue guidance below $2.125bn, or Kratos funded backlog falling below $2.07bn with book-to-bill under 1.0.
Watch nextThe continuing resolution expires 11 December, with AeroVironment's second fiscal-quarter report due in early December.
ValuationAeroVironment 2.09x forward sales and 27.7x forward earnings against roughly 6x sales a year ago; Kratos 2.99x forward sales against about 12x in May.

November 24, 2026 · 2:26 PM IST

Entegris's Per-Wafer Materials Growth Went From 6% to 20% in Three Quarters

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Chip equipment and materials stocks were marked down together this month as though a single tool-buying cycle governed all of them. Entegris, which supplies filtration, chemical-mechanical polishing slurries and specialty chemicals consumed inside working fabs, told investors on 29 October that roughly 70% of its revenue is paid per wafer and per process layer, and that line accelerated from about 6% growth in the first quarter to 20% in the third, roughly twice the wafer-start growth it expects for the year. Gross margin reached 49.7%.

The de-rating landed on three different ways of getting paid for the same wafers. ASML's system prices were agreed before shipment and management says existing backlog does not reprice. Axcelis is the one with genuinely soft trailing numbers, gross margin at 41.0% against 46.1% in early 2025, even as its bookings hit their best level since 2023.

Entegris crossed a billion dollars of quarterly sales for the first time on 29 October, and almost none of it came from chipmakers buying machines. The Billerica, Massachusetts supplier of filtration, slurries and advanced materials handling reported net sales of $1,006m against a consensus near $924m, up 25% from a year earlier and 14% sequentially, with non-GAAP earnings of $1.23 a share.

That matters because the November selling in semiconductor capital equipment treated the whole shelf as one order cycle. Across a nineteen-name group of equipment and materials suppliers, the thirty days to 23 November averaged a loss of about 8%, with fifteen of the nineteen lower and the worst damage in back-end test and components, Teradyne down 24% and FormFactor down 17%. Entegris was one of four that did not fall. Its business is not paid when a tool is ordered; it is paid when a wafer runs.

Entegris bills the fab every wafer it runs

Management puts roughly 30% of revenue as capital-expenditure driven, which leaves about 70% tied to units and layers. "Unit-driven revenue accelerated from approximately 6% in the first quarter to 20% in the third quarter, that is roughly twice the rate of underlying wafer start growth we expect for the year," chief executive Dave Reeder told investors on 29 October. The gap is layer count and tighter contamination control per wafer, not more equipment: more process steps mean more filtration passes and more slurry.

The margin moved with it. Gross margin reached 49.7% in the September quarter from 46.9% in the first, and Reeder credited execution rather than price: "We've improved adjusted gross margin by 530 basis points year-over-year, independent of any pricing action." Backlog rose 35% sequentially and doubled year on year, book-to-bill ran above 1.0, and polishing-slurry growth stepped up to the upper teens from low single digits. The company also won extreme-ultraviolet filtration content at the 2-nanometer node.

The shares are cheaper per dollar of gross profit than they were six months ago: 13.1x trailing gross profit, against 16.4x in May and 14.5x in mid-August, while trailing gross profit grew 42.4%.

ASML's prices were agreed before the tools ship

ASML, the sole supplier of extreme-ultraviolet lithography, is paid out of a book written years in advance. September-quarter revenue rose 55.2% to €11.662bn with gross margin of 57.4%, all EUV output through 2027 is sold, and non-current customer advances, cash for tools due more than a year out, jumped to €9.30bn from €3.57bn in one quarter. "Given the dynamics of this quarter, we now anticipate that our current planned levels of output in 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers," chief financial officer Roger Dassen said on 14 October. Service and upgrades on installed tools added €3.3bn, about 28% of the quarter. ASML trades at 22.8x trailing gross profit against 31.4x in early May.

Axcelis, which sells ion implanters, is the one where the trailing line actually deteriorated. Full-year 2025 revenue fell 17.6% to $839.0m, and gross margin was 41.0% in the September quarter against 46.1% in the first quarter of 2025, a miss management attributed to sharp Korean won appreciation. Yet bookings of $222m produced a 1.5x book-to-bill, its best since late 2023, and China held at 46% of revenue, flat on the prior quarter. At 8.1x trailing gross profit against 10.9x in early May, it is the cheapest of the three and sits 48% below its 52-week high.

Beta did most of the work

To 23 November, ASML was down 12.0% over thirty days and Axcelis 5.7%, while Entegris was up 5.6%. Measured to the 20 November trough three days earlier, the same window reads -22.4%, -20.1% and -12.9%. On 23 November the three rose 9.3%, 14.1% and 11.3% as the market stepped back into AI names, roughly two to three times the 4.7% gain in the S&P 500 tracker, having fallen with it when the index dropped 3.6% on 20 November.

So the month explains itself as a valuation event amplified by beta, not an order event. No pushout, cancellation or sub-1.0 book-to-bill appears in any of the three disclosures. The split between them is in how each would feel a real slowdown: ASML's agreed slots and prepayments mean its 2027 revenue is largely contracted and, management says, does not reprice; Entegris collects on wafers already running in cleanrooms already built; Axcelis has to sell a machine, which is why its trailing revenue fell while its forward book inflected.

The constraint Axcelis chief executive Russell Low named on 5 November cuts both ways for the consumables case. He is watching "very, very carefully the availability of kind of greenfield clean room space because clearly, you know, today, our customers are often 4 wall constrained." Fabs with no room to add tools still add layers, and Entegris gets paid for every one of them. But Reeder's own caution was that units from genuinely new fabs land in 2028 and 2029, which is a long time to be paid by the layer.

The setup

Where it standsEntegris is up 5.6% over thirty days while its equipment shelf averaged a loss near 8%, with about 70% of its revenue paid per wafer and layer.
Would confirmEntegris fourth-quarter sales inside $1.025-1.055bn with gross margin 49.2-49.7%, and unit-driven growth again above wafer-start growth.
Would invalidateEntegris book-to-bill under 1.0, backlog giving back its 35% sequential gain, or a Q1 2027 guide below 20% year-on-year growth.
Watch nextFourth-quarter prints against company guidance: Entegris $1.025-1.055bn, ASML €14.2-15.2bn, Axcelis about $275m; Axcelis-Veeco close expected by Q1 2027.
ValuationEntegris at 13.1x trailing gross profit and 12.3x forward, against 16.4x in May 2026 and 14.5x in mid-August; ASML 22.8x, Axcelis 8.1x.

Fair Isaac Charged More for Fewer Score Pulls; the Regulator Took the Price Lever Away

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Fair Isaac's credit-score business just had the best year in its history, and the mechanism behind it has been capped by the agency that oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Scores revenue rose 41% in the fiscal year ended 30 September while mortgage score pull volumes fell high single digits, so the growth was per-score price.

The Federal Housing Finance Agency opened the same mortgage pull to VantageScore 4.0 for all approved lenders in September and then folded it onto Classic FICO's single loan-price grid, removing the handicap that had made the cheaper score worth less. FICO responded by holding its $10 wholesale price flat for 2027 against a $0.99 alternative and declining to guide fiscal 2027 at all.

Trailing numbers do not explain a 58.6% twelve-month fall; consensus revenue growth of 2.5% for 2027 does.

Fair Isaac, which licenses the FICO credit score into lenders' transaction flows and sells decision-management software to banks, grew its Scores business by more than two-fifths in the fiscal year ended 30 September while being paid for fewer mortgage score pulls than a year earlier. Scores revenue reached $1.652bn, up 41%, and in the September quarter alone mortgage-origination score revenue rose 72% even as unit volumes fell high single digits. The growth was price.

That is a defensible way to run a business when the buyer has no alternative, and until this autumn the buyer did not. FICO's wholesale royalty on a mortgage-origination score went from about 60 cents to $10 over roughly five years, including a doubling for 2026 from $4.95, while Experian and TransUnion offer a VantageScore 4.0 mortgage score at $0.99. The gap did not matter while government-sponsored enterprise loan pricing treated the two scores unequally.

A ten-to-one price gap stopped being academic

On 9 September the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to let all approved lenders use VantageScore 4.0, removing the prior-written-approval requirement after a four-month pilot with 50 lenders. VantageScore 4.0 was already used to securitise about 9% of Fannie and Freddie mortgages between 1 May and 31 August. Then, on 28 September, FHFA director Bill Pulte said the enterprises would merge their two loan-level pricing grids into one, with VantageScore 4.0 joining the Classic FICO grid from 1 October. The prior arrangement effectively required a VantageScore roughly 20 points higher to earn the same loan price; the single grid ends that.

FICO's shares fell 29.2% close-to-close the next session, from $846.22 to $599.51, its worst day since 1989. In October the company launched the FICO Preferred Program, bundling Classic FICO with FICO Score 10T and holding the $10 wholesale price flat for 2027 for lenders agreeing to pull FICO on all applications. It then declined to issue fiscal-2027 guidance, citing unresolved mortgage pricing negotiations and weak loan volumes.

Chief executive William Lansing was blunt about what the company has learned. "I think that transparency and detail on our programs and pricing have not been particularly helpful for FICO," he told investors on 4 November. "On a go-forward basis, our intention is to not share every detail. We're not going to share every pricing program. We're not going to share what the prices are."

The trailing numbers argue the other way

Nothing in the reported results looks like a company in trouble. Revenue grew 13.5%, then 15.9%, then 27.3% across the last three fiscal years to $2.535bn; gross margin widened from 79.7% to 86.1%; free cash flow rose 40% to $1.034bn. The software side is compounding independently of mortgages, with Platform annual recurring revenue of $453m, up 72%, and net revenue retention on that platform of 156%. FICO repurchased $3.028bn of stock, about a tenth of the shares, which left shareholders' equity negative and leverage at 3.29x before buybacks paused in the fourth quarter to repay term debt.

Against that record the shares are 58.6% lower than a year ago and 60.8% below their December peak. Twelve months ago the stock carried roughly 66x trailing earnings; it now carries 19.8x trailing and 16.3x forward.

The forward estimates are where the two pictures reconcile. Consensus models fiscal 2027 revenue of $2.592bn, growth of 2.5% after 27.3%, with net income down 4.3% and earnings per share up 3.8% to $44.27 across a range of $40.41 to $49.04. On those numbers the step from trailing to forward multiple is share count, not growth. A 16x multiple on a business compounding at low single digits with negative book equity is not obviously cheap; it is cheap only against FICO's own history.

Volumes make the point harder. The Mortgage Bankers Association forecast total single-family originations of $2.2tn in 2026, up about 8% from roughly $2.0tn, so a high-single-digit decline in score pulls is worse than the market behind it. Management attributed the decline to elevated rates and said there had been no meaningful loss to competition; the mix also shifted from first-lien mortgages toward lower-priced home equity lines.

What was priced, and what the shelf did not price

The 20.7% recovery from the September low is the market handicapping the defence rather than dismissing it. FICO has signed direct licences with resellers representing roughly 73% of mortgage reseller volume, and its 10T Adopter Program covers 84 lenders with $684bn of eligible annual originations, with the Federal Housing Administration making 10T available from 1 January 2027. Conforming-market use still awaits enterprise sign-off. "10T is the best score available," Lansing said on 4 November. "Everyone is waiting for GSEs to sign off finally so that the conforming market can use it."

This is not a sector being marked down for software disruption. Over the same thirty days to 23 November, Vertex, which sells corporate indirect-tax software and raised full-year guidance on e-invoicing growth, rose 16.4%; Tyler Technologies, the public-sector software vendor, rose 4.2%; Q2 Holdings, which sells digital banking to community institutions and lifted guidance on 12% revenue growth, fell 4.1%. Over twelve months those three are down between 6% and 10.2%. BlackLine, which automates the accounting close, is the other broken name at -54%, and its cause is its own: a 25.1% one-session fall on 6 November after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $195m to $197m against consensus near $207.8m, with dollar-based net revenue retention of 103.5%.

FICO's de-rating, then, is not a multiple catching down to a weak business. It is the market repricing one line of a strong one: a royalty that behaved like a regulated toll and now faces a competing bid at a tenth of the price on the same pull. How much of Scores' 41% growth repeats depends on how many lenders enrol in a program whose terms the company has just said it will stop disclosing.

The next twelve months of that negotiation will happen in private, by design. Investors will learn the outcome the way they learned this one: from a revenue line, after the fact.

Originating hypothesis

sustained bear streak per unit pricing mechanics · subject: FICO, BL

Financial-services software is the one technology shelf on this watchlist where the price action and the label disagree — the category is -6.9% over 30 days and -25.8% over twelve months while still carrying a "still bullish" trend tag, and the damage is concentrated in two starred names moving in opposite directions: Fair Isaac has now held a strongly bearish band for 109 consecutive days (mildly bullish to strongly bearish across the 365-day window) while BlackLine has climbed out of strongly bearish into mildly bearish over both the 30- and 180-day windows — and the question is mechanical rather than directional: establish what one unit of revenue actually is at each business today, since FICO is paid a royalty on every credit score pulled and has been raising the per-score wholesale price into a weak mortgage-origination market just as the regulator opened the same pull to a competing score, while BlackLine sells seat-and-subscription accounting automation whose durability lives in ARR, net revenue retention and platform migration rather than in per-transaction volume.

AI Research Seats Pay Gartner $220,000 a Head and Data Labeling Pays Innodata $14,100

Hypothesis Opus 5 · Research Opus 5 · Writing Opus 5 · Prompt v1.7

Two companies on the same information-services shelf are paid for the same thing — helping enterprises make sense of artificial intelligence — and the unit economics are not remotely comparable. Gartner sells annual research subscriptions at a 71.2% gross margin; Innodata builds and labels training data by the task at 37.2%, down from 46.1% three months earlier.

Gartner's contract value grew 2.5% on a currency-neutral basis to $5.3bn, its third straight quarterly acceleration, and the shares still fell 13.2% in the earnings session. Innodata's revenue rose 52.9% year on year while gross profit fell 16.3% sequentially and its historically largest customer ended a program.

The erosion at Gartner is visible and slow — wallet retention of 98% and 99%. The shock at Innodata is concentrated: two customers were 41% and 32% of nine-month revenue.

Gartner raised every line of its 2026 guidance on 3 November, reported contract value growth accelerating for a third consecutive quarter, and lost 13.2% of its market value in the session. Two days later Innodata, which builds and labels the training and evaluation data that frontier artificial-intelligence labs consume, reported revenue up more than half from a year earlier and gross profit down 16.3% from the prior quarter. Both sell work created by the same force. Neither is paid for it the same way.

The assumption underneath both share prices is that generative models absorb the labor of interpreting information, so the firms selling that interpretation shrink. What the filings show is a question of price per unit rather than volume. Gartner's Stamford-based research, conferences and consulting business converted $1,504.8m of third-quarter revenue into $1,071.6m of gross profit, a 71.2% margin, 230 basis points wider than a year earlier. Innodata's Q3 revenue of $95.6m carried a 37.2% gross margin, against 46.1% in the prior quarter. Annualized across the 19,460 and 10,064 people each company employs, that is roughly $220,000 of gross profit per Gartner employee and $14,100 per Innodata employee — a derived figure, and a fifteen-fold gap between renting a seat and delivering a dataset.

The substitution at Gartner is in the wallet, not the logo

Gartner's 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 September reports Global Technology Sales contract value up 2% year on year, driven primarily by new clients, with client retention improving to 85% from 84%. Wallet retention — what existing clients spend against the prior year — was 98%. In the business-functions segment it was 99% against 104% a year earlier, and the filings attribute the decline to lower spending by existing clients. Clients are staying and buying slightly less. US federal work is 2% to 3% of the contract value base, too small to carry the move.

"One of the things that we are seeing now is clients coming back to us and sort of saying, 'Wow, it is a lot harder than I thought to get any benefits from AI. I have got the cost, but not the benefits,'" chairman and chief executive Gene Hall said on the 3 November call. Chief financial officer Craig Safian was blunter about the trajectory: "We fully expect the CV growth rate in total to accelerate from where we are today." The 2026 price increase, effective 1 November, was 3%, the low end of the company's historical 3% to 4% range.

The socket is shrinking around a share gainer. Forrester, Gartner's nearest listed rival, reported third-quarter contract value of $281.9m, down 3.5%, revenue of $86.1m against $94.3m, and client retention of 78%.

Innodata's volume held and its per-task price did not

Innodata's growth barely decelerated — 54.4%, 57.8% and 52.9% across the first three quarters of 2026 — while gross profit growth fell from 82.7% in Q2 to 37.3% in Q3. Operating income declined 19.6% year on year as revenue grew.

Then the mechanics arrived. Around 550 staff in India were terminated on 26 October, with further cuts in the Philippines, a termination email citing a "ramp-down of the business assignment" rather than performance; the shares fell 25.3% the next session. On 5 November management disclosed that the historically largest customer had ended one program in mid-October, a roughly $12m revenue headwind in the fourth quarter. The September 10-Q puts 73% of nine-month revenue in two accounts, at 41% and 32%.

The replacement book is contractual. A customer under 5% of revenue a year ago became the largest, signing a $29m pre-training data program plus roughly $18m more; another hyperscaler went from $3.1m of trailing-twelve-month revenue to programs chief executive Rahul Singhal said "may contribute more than $20 million in revenue in 2027". Full-year growth guidance went up, to 42% or more. Innodata ended the quarter with $153.7m of cash net of customer prepayments and no debt.

It is also the small vendor in its own market. Private trackers size the expert-data business at about $2.6bn in 2026, with Mercor near $2bn of annualized gross revenue, Surge AI about $1.4bn and Scale AI around $1bn against Innodata's roughly $382m run rate; Mercor raised $750m at a $20bn valuation, some eighteen times Innodata's $1.1bn market capitalization.

What each decline is actually pricing

Gartner's shares fetch 2.48x gross profit on both trailing and forward numbers, against roughly 4.0x a year ago and about 10x at the 2025 high; the de-rating exceeds the 24.9% fall in the price because $1.7bn of buybacks cut the diluted share count 14.7%. Consensus has low-single-digit revenue growth with double-digit earnings growth, which is margin and share count doing the work. Barclays' Manav Patnaik cut the stock to Underweight on 6 November while raising his target to $185 from $150, calling per-seat exposure "already too high for a world in which the macro pressures are likely to continue".

Innodata trades at 7.65x trailing gross profit, down from roughly 18.3x a year ago and about 29x in late May. Its forward earnings multiple of 27.2x sits above the trailing 21.9x, because consensus full-year earnings of $1.18 against $1.12 already reported implies about $0.06 in the fourth quarter — the $12m headwind, priced.

So the shelf-level slide blends two unlike events. Gartner's renewal base is eroding by one or two points of wallet a year while gross margin widens and the share count shrinks, which is why a quarter that beat could still cost a quarter of the equity: the market marked down the terminal growth rate of a seat, not this year's cash. Innodata's problem is narrower and sharper — the volume of AI data work is still compounding, but the price per task fell nine points of margin in a single quarter and two customers decide the revenue line.

Hall's clients are now paying Gartner to tell them why their AI spending has not paid off. Innodata is paid to build the thing they bought. One invoice renews every twelve months at 3% more; the other ends when a program does, by email, mid-shift.

SPX Technologies, which builds Marley and Recold evaporative cooling towers and fluid coolers for industrial and data-center heat rejection, told investors on 29 October that the order book in its cooling business had reached a record and that filling it cost more than planned. Both halves were true at once. The heating, ventilation and air-conditioning backlog stood at $1,102.5m at the end of the September quarter, up 69% year on year organically and 15% sequentially, with more than 90% of the data-center work tied to hyperscale customers. Segment margin fell about 140 basis points.

That print has been read as the first crack in the thermal-demand story that carried the shares through 2025. The disclosure does not support it. Group revenue rose 20.5% to $714.5m, HVAC revenue rose 35.5%, and management reaffirmed that capacity projects remain on track to support roughly $1.1bn of annual data-center revenue at full production. What deteriorated was the cost of shipping, not the demand behind it.

The hiring bill, priced at five cents

Chief financial officer Mark Carano put about $15m of the quarter's shortfall on growth-related labor and outsourcing inefficiency and about $10m on input-cost inflation, and Truist cut its price target to $233 from $266 on 2 November on that margin pressure while keeping a Buy rating; JPMorgan went to $190 from $225 on 11 November. The spending was deliberate. "We made a decision, it was an intentional decision to kind of accelerate our hiring and secure additional suppliers to ensure that we can meet the demand that's out there really for the balance of this year and really set us up for next year," Carano said on the 29 October call. SPX also has price increases embedded in the backlog and frame agreements with hyperscalers that adjust for material input-cost moves, which is why management does not frame this as a pricing failure.

The arithmetic of the blemish: the top of the full-year adjusted earnings range came down to $8.50, taking the midpoint to $8.35, a five-cent reduction. Full-year revenue guidance of $2.745–2.805bn still implies about 23% growth at the midpoint.

The selling came a week later, and not from SPX

The shares closed at $163.45 on 3 November and $142.71 on 6 November, a 12.7% fall across three sessions with no company disclosure in between. On 5 November the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.4% as investors dumped chip and data-center names, on fears of construction restrictions after the midterms, hyperscaler capex of $720–740bn against negative free cash flow, and CoreWeave credit-default spreads at record wides. SPX closed at a 52-week low of $136.29 on 20 November and $145.37 on 23 November, 41% below its 52-week high close and down 28.9% over twelve months. The likelier reading is that the market is discounting the conversion of a construction backlog whose customers' financing just repriced, rather than the backlog itself.

The move was not SPX's alone: Vertiv fell 26% and Modine 27% over three months against SPX's 27.9%. Within heat rejection for data centers, SPX's rivals are private: it, Baltimore Aircoil and EVAPCO together hold about half the 2025 data-center cooling-tower market by value.

The component suppliers kept their ratings

Dover, the diversified industrial whose Climate & Sustainability Technologies segment sells SWEP brazed-plate heat exchangers and quick-disconnect couplings, reported segment revenue of $481.5m, up 18% organically, with bookings up 43.1% to $594.1m — a book-to-bill of 1.23 — and segment margin down to 16.7% from 18.6% on footprint consolidation. Dover put data-center growth at 30% for 2026 and SWEP lead times at about 25 weeks, with capacity in the main data-center line doubling by mid-2027. Its shares are unchanged over three months, at 19.0 times forward earnings against 23.5 times trailing.

Parker-Hannifin, the motion-and-control group whose Quick Coupling Division competes with Dover's couplings, reported record quarterly sales of $5.992bn and raised full-year guidance. Management put data centers at about 1.5% of sales and "not yet large enough to be its own vertical" — roughly $380m on the coming year's consensus base. Parker is the dearest of the three at 24.8 times forward earnings, and 13.7 times trailing gross profit against 15.6 times in August.

What five cents explains

The guidance cut accounts for a fraction of a percent of SPX's earnings power and none of a 28% twelve-month decline. On the business, the direction is the other way: orders at a record, organic cooling growth guided near 30% for the second half, and $1.2bn spent on four HVAC acquisitions plus FIS Water this year for roughly $310m of combined revenue run-rate at a blended 11.7 times, leaving leverage near 1.8x. The shares now carry 17.3 times forward earnings against 24.5 times in August.

Two things keep the doubt open. Consensus revenue of $2.779bn for 2026 sits near the top of management's own range, so the forward figure rests on execution of the ramp that just cost $15m. And a backlog of cooling towers is a claim on halls that are not yet energized — the one thing the 5 November repricing questioned.

SPX's non-data-center markets are mixed: power, industrial, semiconductor and pharma strong, education, government and new commercial soft. The company is being valued as though the 90% of its data-center book that belongs to hyperscalers is the fragile part.

In October SPX fell to a 52-week low and the explanation offered was Nvidia's claim that its next rack generation needs no chillers. The low is 13% lower now, and the disclosure since then has been a record order book and a hiring bill. Whatever is being priced, it is not the quarter SPX reported.
